newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.African analysts back wider interest rate debate.
newsitem.headline: S.African analysts back wider interest rate debate.

text.p: South African economists on Tuesday welcomed the burgeoning public debate about the role of the independent central bank, but said monetary policy should be kept outside the political arena.

President Nelson Mandela's African National Congress (ANC) has fueled the debate with a draft strategy document urging the inclusion of monetary policy in the government's economic strategy for growth and development.
The influential Congress of South African Trade Unions (Cosatu), a partner of the ANC in government, is demanding that interest rates should be set in consultation with the cabinet.
"It is appropriate that there should be more transparency and more public debate on monetary policy," said Jac Laubscher, chief economist for the Sanlam investment institution.
"But we must recognise that for an emerging economy, the independence and the international standing of the central bank is one of the key points watched by foreign investors."
Dave Mohr, chief economist for Old Mutual, the country's biggest investment institution, also welcomed the debate, but cautioned against handing monetary policy to politicians.
"It's a job that's in the domain of the economists.... Monetary policy is not something that we should leave to politicians and people with vested interests," he said.
Last week Labour Minister Tito Mboweni told Reuters in an interview that interest-rate policy should be part of the government's job-creation strategy.
On Monday Transport Minister Mac Maharaj, a senior ANC policy-maker, called the Reserve Bank "an isolated pocket of power" that should consult more widely on monetary policy.
He said the ANC would not tinker with the constitutional independence of the Bank, but would encourage consultation with the finance ministry and other interest groups.

"There is a legitimate point of separation so that there is focused attention (on monetary policy), but there is also a legitimate point of interdependence between your broad economic policy and how you manage monetary and fiscal policy," he said.
Reserve Bank Governor Chris Stals, who is under sustained left-wing fire for holding the key interest rate at 17 percent since last November, gave some ground at the weekend.
He told Business Day he would not oppose the expansion of the bank's internal four-person sub-committee that manages monetary policy to include "sensible" outside advisors.
"I don't have a serious problem (with that) and, because of the accusations that I am a power on my own, maybe it would be better to have a broader committee," he said.
An economist for a major bank, who asked not to be named, said there was an unspoken international perception that African economies were more vulnerable to interference than others.
"If the ANC were to be seen to compromise the independence of the central bank, it would be the start of a slippery slide.

"African countries have not had a very good history on monetary policy. It probably would not be stated, but the worry would be that this is another African country and as an African country one has to be cleaner than clean," he said.
The economist supported the suggestion of an expanded Reserve Bank sub-committee on monetary policy, but added:
"The issue would be who they put on the committee. If they included in that panel some of the wilder boys from Cosatu, for example, that would also be construed negatively."
Old Mutual's Mohr said expanding the sub-committee could promote transparency, adding:
"It could be a healthy development provided that you have good, sound professional economists on the committee.
"What would be dangerous would be to have a set of cabinet ministers deciding on interest rate policies," he said.
The central bank's exclusive control over monetary policy will be on the agenda at the conferences of the ANC, Cosatu and the South African Communist Party between now and December.
